blocks.text: Witness statement of SHELLEY TOMLINS (read)
My Lord, some statements to read to conclude the evidence relating to the 13th into 14 October and event 3, as it's been described to the jury.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: I begin, please, with a statement to be read from Shelley Tomlins, which is page 77 in my Lord's bundle.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: Shelley Tomlins provided a statement on 13 June 2019 in which she says:
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "I have been asked by DC Birch from Cheshire Police about my recollections of and involvement with a baby called [Baby I], who died on 23 October 2015 at the Countess of Chester Hospital.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "I have been asked in particular about 29 September 2015 and 14 October 2015. Prior to providing the statement, I have had the opportunity to review [Baby I]'s clinical notes and I make this statement based on those notes and my own personal recollection.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "I do remember [Baby I]. I can't remember exactly how premature she was, but I remember she initially came in from another hospital because I think I was the first one who initially looked after her when she arrived at Chester.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "I remember her family and looking after her multiple times. I can't remember the intricate details, but remember she had ongoing respiratory distress you might associate with being premature, and definitely had feeding and gut problems. I also remember she had problems with a distended abdomen.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "I remember someone saying they thought she had strictures, I think because she possibly had NEC in the past. It was like there was scar tissue in her bowel, which meant there was narrowing. She stopped tolerating feeds and it was like there were blockages in her bowels, which meant she would get really distended. It was probably one of the medical team talking about it, but I can't remember who it was. It may have come from surgeons looking at X-rays of her bowel.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "With regards to 29 September 2015, I was on a long day and I was the designated nurse for [Baby I]. The notes state that at 08.00 hours I took over care for the long day, she was selfventilating in air, her Masimo monitoring had been discontinued the day before, and an apnoea alarm was in place. My notes say she was slightly constipated and straining to open her bowels. She was mottled in appearance. Mottling is when a person's skin looks a little bit like corned beef. It is purplish-white, like when someone is really cold. It's a bit blotchy. In my experience I can say that some babies can look like that all the time and sometimes it can be a sign that they are a little bit unwell, for example if their perfusion is not that good.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "She wasn't on very much monitoring at that time and was just feeding and in a hot cot rather than an incubator. That would indicate to me that she was clothed and I would have to remove her clothing to change her nappy throughout the day and generally have a look at her whole body. My notes don't detail exactly where her mottling was on her body but it was probably her whole body, although I can't say for certain.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "With regards to 14 October 2015, I was on a long day. My first notes were written at 9.22, but I came on duty at 07.30. We hand over from 07.30 to 8.00 in the morning but I think I went straight in to get a bedside handover at 0.7.30 from Lucy Letby
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: because [Baby I] wasn't well and there was going to be a lot to talk about.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Lucy was probably already at the bedside when I walked into nursery 1, but I can't be 100% sure. I remember standing with Lucy at the bedside and we had started the handover. I don't remember how long we got into the handover or how much I was told, but we were talking about her and she had a cardiac arrest right when we were looking at her.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "In terms of who was in the room, there was Yvonne Farmer, who I remember because I think I drew up the medications, including adrenaline, with her during the resus. There was Jo Williams and she did chest compressions. There was Matt Neame, who was the registrar and who was leading the resus. Her mum and dad were there, potentially Laura Eagles may have been, but I can't be sure.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "After a little while, Ravi Jayaram, a consultant, arrived. My notes state that I arrived on the unit minutes before the arrest. [Baby I] had just been re-tubed when she desaturated and bradycardia occurred. Full resuscitation was required to bring her back and I wrote 'See medical notes for full details", which meant the doctor's notes.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "She was then stable on a ventilator with a size 3 ETT, which was 7.5 centimetres at the lips, pulled back by half a centimetre by Dr Jayaram, one of the consultants. Her ventilator pressures were 28/5 and the rate was 40 with an increased respiratory time of 0.5 seconds."
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: She says:
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "It actually says '0.5 centimetres' but that's an error by me.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "She had a fluid allowance of 150ml per kilogram per day. She had 10% dextrose infusing through a peripheral cannula and morphine and dobutamine infusing through a long line in her right leg. The site was satisfactory.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "She had a previous extravasation burn on her right arm from her resuscitation on 13 October. A cannula is supposed to be in the vein but giving fluids and drugs through it will burn the tissue if it isn't going via the right route.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "I recorded that she passed urine and had a small bowel movement and that her abdomen was very large, pale and veiny, with an umbilical hernia evident.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "I noted an area of discolouration. If it was mottling I would have written it down if that's what it was. I would describe
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: discolouration as slightly greyish in colour and would have been darker than the rest of her body.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "I noted that pancuronium was administered at 08.30 because [Baby I] was difficult to ventilate and desaturating and also notes that her antibiotics from the night shift were only half given due to her collapse and that doctors were aware.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "My next notes were written retrospectively at 17.08 hours. I recorded that her ventilation was weaned steadily throughout the day due to over-ventilated gases. At that time she was on 16/4, with a rate of 35, and a respiratory time of 0.4 seconds. She had good air entry bilaterally (both lungs) and suction had yielded only a small amount of clear secretions -- that's suction of mucus from inside the breathing tube.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Her oxygen requirements dropped to 24%, but had recently raised to 35% following handling for intravenous access. That happens when you move the baby around as you can stress them out.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Attempts at long lines and cannulas had been unsuccessful and therefore the plan was to wean dobutamine as tolerated and discontinue it as soon as possible. Her blood pressure mean was in the 50s and she was to have bloods taken later that day. We would have to move midazolam to another intravenous port due to infusion incompatibilities. We were also waiting for urine and electrolyte results as we were checking her for low potassium and potentially run a potassium infusion through a central long line.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "She did settle well throughout the day after the start she'd had. My next notes are 20.27 that evening. Her blood pressure mean remained satisfactory, therefore dobutamine was discontinued at 18.00 hours. Midazolam was running centrally, leaving peripheral access free for blood transfusion and antibiotics. The potassium infusion was never commenced due to difficulties with access and also because her levels rose slightly. Her latest potassium from gases was 3.2 and her capillary blood gas was good at 19.15 hours. We did not commence her on ciprofloxacin due to it being unavailable.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "I noted that her mum and dad were present during the day with her siblings and I also noted that after advice from Alder Hey surgeons, we may need to remove free air from her bowel using a tube or something if her tummy was to blow up again. I think it was because of the morning when I came on and her bowel had blown up so massive that it was compressing her lungs and I think that's what caused her to collapse. It was massive and I don't know at what point it went like that, but it was what caused the arrest so I imagine it would have been there at 07.30 hours.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "I remember thinking during the resus that morning that we'd lost her as it was a long time, almost 15 minutes. I think the parents thought that too. They were there for all the resus. Someone must have called them, but I can't remember if they were already there at handover when I got there.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "That day sticks in my mind because it was the last ever shift I did at the hospital as I left a few days after it."
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: Witness statement of MS JOANNE WILLIAMS (read)
My Lord, the next statement is that of Joanne Williams at page 81.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: This statement is dated 25 June 2018:
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "DC Birch from Cheshire Police asked me about the night of 13 October into the morning of 14 October and my recollections of and involvement with [Baby I].
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "I had looked after [Baby I] when she first came to Chester so I knew her and her family. She left Chester on a couple of occasions and I looked after her on her first return to the unit, I think, but since then I hadn't been her nurse.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "With regards to the 13 October night shift, rotas show me working with Caroline Oakley, Laura Eagles and Lucy Letby. There may also have been a band 4 nurse on but I'm not sure. I wasn't [Baby I]'s designated nurse that night.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "I have had the chance to review the notes and, from memory, have a very brief recollection of helping with chest compressions on [Baby I] that night. I have checked our records and I did not book any drugs out with regards to [Baby I] on the 13th into 14 October. Even having read the notes, I can't remember what time the collapse happened. In addition to being involved in chest compressions, I can remember where she was in the nursery and her mum being there, but other than that I can't recall anything else.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "With regards to where she was in the nursery, she was in nursery 1 and in the middle of the room."
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: Witness statement of MS LAURA EAGLES (read)

My Lord, back to page 64, please, for the next statement, that of Laura Eagles. It's one of those statements, my Lord, of which we read part of an earlier event, so it's the statement dated 24 October 2019.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: I go to 64:
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "I was also asked by DC Birch about the dates of the 13th into 14 October 2015 in relation to [Baby I]. Again, I've had the opportunity to go through the notes and I could see that she had two collapses, one at 07.00 and one at 07.45 on the 14th.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "I don't really remember anything too specific from that night, such as who was where and who did that. I wasn't looking after [Baby I]. Lucy Letby was her designated nurse and I know that from reading the notes. Caroline Oakley was in charge of the unit that night and I was looking after an ITU baby, an HDU baby and another sick baby.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "I'm sure I would have come to help but it was very busy. Jo Williams and Janet Cox were also on and from our Badger system I could see there were three ITU babies, two HDU babies and seven special care babies that night.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "I have been informed that I co-signed for two lots of sodium chloride, which is a bolus, for [Baby I] at 06.28 hours and 06.35 hours on 14 October, but I was unable to see that when I looked at the notes as it is recorded on the electronic medication administration record."
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: They are the forms that we'll see, very different from the nursing notes, on the sequence of events chart:
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "We don't have access to those once babies are discharged. Also I have been told I co-signed for teicoplanin, an antibiotic, at 06.27 hours that day. Again, I couldn't see that as it was on EMAR. I can look at the scanned paper prescriptions but not at my electronic signatures.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "From the notes I can see [Baby I] was re-intubated at 07.00 hours, but she really didn't pick back up significantly and by 07.45 hours CPR was commenced. I don't think she particularly recovered from the 07.00 collapse, so the 07.45 hours was a continuation of that first collapse.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "I don't really have recollections of that but I obviously signed for drugs and so was clearly involved at some level. I remember [Baby I] well. I just don't remember all of the events. She was ill several times and was on the unit a long time. It is hard to say which one was which and each event is hard to separate from another within my memory."
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: My Lord, that concludes Laura Eagles' statement.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: Witness statement of DR DAVID HARKNESS (read)

We can return, please, to Dr Harkness, who -- and in particular page 73 of my Lord's bundle. Again, picking up his statement, part of which we've already read and which is dated 17 October 2018, Dr Harkness says this:
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "She [meaning [Baby I]] had quite an eventful night overnight on the 13th into the 14th. Looking at the notes, her oxygen requirements had gone up a bit. She needed chest X-rays again with possibly some collapse of her lung. She had had a new endotracheal tube for ventilation to see whether that would help and that seemed to improve things at that point in time. Then she deteriorated again and the worry seems to be from the notes that there was a pneumothorax there and Dr Jayaram had been called. She carried on deteriorating and she needed CPR in the early hours of that morning.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "The next entry written by me was on 14 October 2015 at 11.00 hours. This was another ward round routine review. She was 36 weeks plus 5, so day 63 of life. Problems-wise, I wrote that she'd had two cardiac arrests, was on a ventilator and we were suspecting NEC.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "They were quite long arrests as well, 20 minutes or so of resus, which is a long time. At this point she was on relatively high pressures on the ventilator, her oxygen level had come down quite quickly, so one of the medications I gave her that morning was a dose of a paralysis agent, which helped her stop moving and fighting against the ventilator. This can make it easier for them to breathe. Her blood gases were acceptable but not fantastic and were still on the poor side.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Her lactate, which can be a sign of poor perfusion and them being unwell, particularly with things like NEC was 7.6, which is quite high. You'd normally like it to be about 1 or 2.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Examining her, I found some crackle on the left side of the lungs. There had been a suggestion of a bit of a collapse of the lung and those noises pointed to a collapse or infection or fluid on the lung, which may explain why we were struggling with ventilation. We had her on some fluids via the lines with no TPN or feeds. She had opened her bowels and had good urine output of 3.8ml per kilogram per hour. You want to see more than 1 millilitre per kilogram per hour. This is a good sign of your blood pressure and your perfusion to your kidneys and organs, so that was good. It suggested her blood pressure was good. She was also on some meds for blood pressure.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "We were still waiting on any blood cultures to see if there was any proof of an infection. Her CRP was 3. CRP can go up with immunisations as well and doesn't always go up in babies with infections. Where CRP is useful is when it is high and if you
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: are treating something, you want to see it coming down. So if you are looking at a trend of it coming down, it suggests that whatever was there is getting better.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Where it is not helpful is when it never goes up. It doesn't mean they haven't got an infection. Her white blood cell count was around 25.6, which is high. You'd normally expect it to be around the 10 mark. That's a sign of infection, inflammation and stress.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "I had also looked at the X-rays at this point, which showed something new, but did show previous changes in chronic lung disease.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "After my entries, there is advice from the Alder Hey surgical team on her the notes. This was a phone call back from one of the surgical consultants discussing [Baby I] with [Dr B], who thought that because she previously may have had an episode of NEC that had been medically treated, she now had a stricture, a narrowing of the gut. The surgical consultants didn't think at this time there was any perforation of the gut and they suggested carrying on for a week on the antibiotics as we were doing, keeping her nil by mouth, and feeding her TPN.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "They said that if the abdomen carried on getting bigger and bigger, to put a tube into the rectum to vent some air off. They also wanted daily X-rays to look for any further signs that this was NEC and it was getting worse. Not just X-ray signs but also from further blood tests, looking at CRP and whether it went up or if platelets came down, which can both be signs of things worsening. Then they would consider doing surgery at that point.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "It was about monitoring her closely and then once she was better they would consider doing some contrast studies where you put radioactive dye into the bowel to look for a narrowing to see if there was anything that was causing problems. If they found something they would have to remove it, but this was all planned for 1 to 2 weeks down the line.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "My next entry was at 16.00 hours the same day, the 14th. Her ventilation was much improved and the pressures on the ventilator had come down nicely. She needed some blood as she was anaemic, but her blood pressure was better so the plan was to stop the dobutamine for that.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "One of the issues we'd had was it had been very difficult for us to get any access to give her anything. The discussion was around giving her blood through the cannula that we were no longer giving her dobutamine through. This was all anticipated to be in the next 12 hours or so.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Again I also summarised the previous conversations [Dr B] had had about the daily X-rays and the surgeons' plan not to restart any feeds and the idea of putting a tube up her bottom to let out any air if we needed to. I don't believe we ever needed to do that. That was just what they had said if her abdomen was so big it affected her breathing by putting pressure on her lungs. It is more common in adults and is often called a flatus tube but we never needed to do that.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "The commonest things that sets things off in premature babies is infection. They are still vulnerable being on a neonatal unit as there are more people and more exposure to bugs, but they're equally not safe at home. Their immune system isn't quite there and so the chance of getting an infection is there. They shouldn't be born yet so the amount of stress on their body means they are more prone to getting something.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "With [Baby I], her CRP had been high and come down. The problem we get is that it is very rare you'll find bacteria in the blood that give you answers. X-rays are only so good at showing us what's going on. They are not good enough or sensitive enough that we can look at them and say exactly what it is that's going on, we look for suggestions of things going on. Her X-rays had never given us the categorical answer that this was NEC. It all suggested there might be this stricture there from a previous episode and it was causing her problems again. We don't know with NEC how often it actually happens and the only way you can confirm it is once you have done the surgery and removed the bowel.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "In a lot of suspected cases you give them antibiotics, you rest their gut and they get better, which was probably what was happening with [Baby I]. Certainly the way she deteriorated with her abdomen becoming distended fits with the abdomen being the cause of the problem. The abdomen got larger and firm and bowel sounds were there but none consistently. She wasn't opening her bowels regularly and it all pointed towards it being related to her bowel.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "In the last week of her life, I don't appear on the clinical notes and I don't know if I was away or working on the children's ward covering. I do remember [Baby I]'s death and I remember her parents coming back to the unit a few times over the next year or so."
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: That concludes Dr Harkness' statement.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: Thank you.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Witness statement of DR SRINVASARO BABARAO (read)
My Lord, there is one more statement to be read in this section from the case from Dr Babarao.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: This is a statement, my Lord, from Dr Srinvasaro Babarao. It's dated 29 March 2019 and it deals with [Baby I]'s transfer on 15 October to the tertiary centre. Dr Babarao says:
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "I am a consultant neonatologist at the Wirral University Teaching Hospital. This is also known as Arrowe Park Hospital. [Baby I], date of birth 7 August 2015, was referred to us at Arrowe Park Hospital from the Countess of Chester on 15 October 2015.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "I was the consultant for the clinical shift on that day covering the neonatal unit. I don't recall the exact conversations I've had prior to transport. However, referring to the medical notes, there were conversations between consultants at Chester, Liverpool Women's Hospital and Arrowe Park Hospital and it was decided that [Baby I] should be sent to Arrowe Park as it was closer to home and we are a tertiary/level 3 unit which cares for such babies.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "[Baby I] was transported by Cheshire and Mersey Neonatal Transport Service. She arrived with us at 15.30 hours approximately on 15 October 2015. There was a routine clerking of the baby as normal practice, as she came on to the unit. She was day 68 of life on that day. Her corrected gestation was 36 plus 6, so 36 weeks and 6 days, having been born at 27 weeks' gestation, with a birth weight of 0.97 kilograms and current weight of 1.83 kilograms.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "The background information was she had respiratory distress syndrome as a preterm, chronic lung disease, again due to prematurity, and there was suspected necrotising enterocolitis (NEC) infection/inflammation of the gut, which is not uncommon in preterm babies.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "[Baby I] had already been discussed with the surgical team at Alder Hey Children's Hospital and the intention was that she would be conservatively managed. There were discussions between the Countess of Chester consultants and the surgical team at Alder Hey Hospital as a plan from the surgical perspective that she may require some contrast studies to look if there were any strictures or obstruction in the gut.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "From the medical notes, I can see that [Baby I] had two cardiac arrests in the 36 hours prior to her arrival at Arrowe Park. There had been a discussion with Liverpool Women's Hospital the previous day to her admission and discussions whether she should be transferred there. However, it was agreed and decided at that
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: time she did not need to be transferred to Liverpool Women's Hospital and remained at Chester.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "The following day, in the early hours of the morning, she had another acute episode of cardiac arrest and, further to this, she was on the ventilator with a breathing tube and the discussions were again to transfer [Baby I].
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "She was accepted by myself to Arrowe Park Hospital for continuing care at a level 3 unit. [Baby I] arrived on 15 October 2015, ventilated with a breathing tube in. It was the appropriate size and correct length. She was on a moderate amount of ventilation and oxygen requirements of 36%, which is not a lot.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "She was kept nil by mouth as per the plan from the Chester neonatal unit. She was on intravenous fluids. This was changed to total parenteral nutrition and lipid, which is what we do for any preterm baby who is nil by mouth via a central line, which is also known as a long line.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "She was also on sedation of midazolam and morphine, which is routine. She had already commenced on antibiotics for necrotising enterocolitis and a possible infection. These were co-amoxiclav, metronidazole and gentamicin.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "On assessment the baby was pink, warm and well perfused and her vital signs were within normal limits. Her abdomen" --
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: Sorry, could you pause there for a moment?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Can I just have a moment, please?
blocks.speaker: JUROR

blocks.text: Certainly, yes. A moment out?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: For a moment if that's okay.
blocks.speaker: JUROR

blocks.text: Yes, certainly. Well, I think... I don't know if it's possible for -- when you say a moment -- JUROR: Just a moment so I can just cool down a little bit.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Yes. You've got some water there, have you and everything? Do you have any tissues?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: I haven't.
blocks.speaker: JUROR

blocks.text: Usher, I think that would help in the first instance, wouldn't it? I don't really want everyone to have to go out if it isn't necessary. Is it possible for you to slip out for a minute to compose yourself?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Does anyone have any objection to this juror -- we'll remain here -- just leaving the court for a moment to compose herself? Thank you very much.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Take as long as you like, we'll wait here.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: (Pause)

I apologise again for the fluctuating temperatures we get here. As I've said several times before, I don't have any real control of it. I try and ask for it to be a median temperature, which is sort of generally acceptable to everyone, but it's impossible to achieve, I'm afraid.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: (Pause)
All right? Just raise your hand if you need another break. If I hear you coughing, I'll look at you, obviously. Thank you.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: I'll go back a little bit, my Lord.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, please, because it was difficult.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: I was not sensitive to it and I'll have another crack at those antibiotics as well when we get there.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: So:
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "[Baby I] arrived on 15 October 2015, ventilated with a breathing tube in, which was the appropriate size and correct length. She was on a moderate amount of ventilation and oxygen requirements of 36%, which is not a lot.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "She was kept nil by mouth as per the plan from Chester neonatal unit. She was on intravenous fluids and this was changed to total parenteral nutrition and lipid, which is what we do for any preterm baby who is nil by mouth via a central line, which is also known as a long line.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "She was also on sedation of midazolam and morphine, which is routine, and she'd [already] commenced on antibiotics for necrotising enterocolitis and a possible infection. These were co-amoxiclav, metronidazole and gentamicin.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "On assessment, the baby was pink, warm and well perfused and her vital signs were within normal limits. Her abdomen was soft, but bowel sounds were not heard, which is not unusual when treating issues with the gut. The plan at the time was to stabilise the baby and to keep her nil by mouth, monitor gases, continue parenteral nutrition, continue antibiotics, and follow
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: the plan by the surgical team at Alder Hey, which was to conservatively manage this episode and this would be 7 days nil by mouth, 7 days of antibiotics and then considered doing a contrast study, which would be done either at Alder Hey Children's Hospital or at Liverpool Women's Hospital.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Routinely, an X-ray would be done if a baby comes to us ventilated. An X-ray was done that evening. It showed the breathing tube to be in a reasonably good position and also showed the long line, the central line, to also be in good position. There are no comments in the notes as to the appearance of the gut, but there are comments that the lungs looked like preterm lungs.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "On 15 October 2015 I finished my duty at 17.00 hours and I was not on call that evening. I had handed over to colleagues. I can see from the senior registrar and the consultant notes from that evening that [Baby I] was stable on the unit until around 00.13 hours on 16 October 2015 when there was a sudden episode of bradycardia and desaturation. This means her heart rate and oxygen levels dropped suddenly following suction through the breathing tube, which is a usual practice that nurses carry out.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "At this time she was Neopuffed, which means she was disconnected from the ventilator and efforts were made to bag her manually through the breathing tube. From the medical notes, there was no improvement of the heart rate with the bagging and there was no chest movement after bagging. The chest should move with bagging unless there is an obstruction or the tube has displaced.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "At this time there was no air entry and the tube position was confirmed using a capnograph. This is where a tiny device is placed on top of the breathing tube to establish if there is any carbon dioxide coming out. If there is, it will trigger a colour change on the device. It did not change colour so it meant the breathing tube was obstructed or had moved from its position, so the safest thing to do is to remove the breathing tube.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "[Baby I]'s tube was removed at this time and was found to be blocked with dark-coloured blood, probably from the previous collapse in Chester. As the tube was removed, she responded very quickly and the heart rate and saturations came up. This confirmed it was the tube that was the problem as it was blocked. Once the tube was removed, it was assessed if she could be re-intubated and the tube put back, but the notes state she was spontaneously breathing and she received positive endexpiratory pressure, PEEP, to support her breathing. She was saturating well and given the fact that she was 36 weeks, nearly 37 weeks, and a good weight, and looking at the respiratory
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: pattern, they decided not to re-intubate her but to try a lower level of respiratory support, which was high flow.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "At this time they also visually checked the oral cavity and the vocal cords where the breathing tube went in to check for any evidence of trauma. They were checking for any ongoing bleeding. The notes mention there was no fresh bleeding or any significant injury noted so they were satisfied to commence with high flow on 5 litres, which is an optimal amount of flow, and she was in about 35% oxygen.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "The parents were updated by the consultants and senior registrar at this time. The following morning, the registrar and junior doctor reviewed [Baby I] at 04.30 am, which was routine. She was stable in high flow, 5 litres, in about 30-35% oxygen. She had very good blood gases, minimal recessions, no issues with her breathing, no respiratory difficulty. The mean blood pressures were fine, urine output was good and she'd been kept nil by mouth.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "[Baby I]'s abdomen was soft and it was not distended and her bowel movements could be heard at this time and it was reassuring that the tummy was fine and not worsening. She hadn't opened her bowels. However, this was not unusual as she'd been kept nil by mouth. A featureless bowel was noted from the X-ray and there was no noted gas from lack of gut movement.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "From the infection perspective, the inflammatory markers were non-impressive. The CRP used in an infection marker was less than 5, which is normal, and the blood cultures from Chester were also negative. The triple antibiotics were continued and [Baby I] was also commenced on a phosphate infusion as the routine blood tests carried out at Arrowe Park did show low phosphate. All other blood tests were reasonable.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "The plan was to leave [Baby I] on high flow and reduce the oxygen as tolerated and keep her for 7 days nil by mouth and continue with triple antibiotics for the 7 days as per the original surgical team plan arranged by Chester.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "The following morning, on 16 October 2015, I was back on duty and a review was completed and notes were made to reduce the phosphate infusion to half the dose as her levels were coming up and to discuss when the contrast studies would happen with relevant surgeons. There was ongoing monitoring of the gases and blood pressure and she was moved to the high dependency unit based on that she was 37 weeks, stable on high flow, and her gases were good. Her oxygen requirements were coming down.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "I had also made a plan that if [Baby I] continued on high flow with no issues, I suggested she should be discussed with Chester for repatriation(?) the following day.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "We had observed the baby. We extubated the baby and she had been stable on low respiratory support and there was no ongoing need for a tertiary level input, so the baby could return to Chester to be closer to home with parents for ongoing care.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Later that day, 16 October 2015, at around 16.45 hours, the call was made to Alder Hey Children's Hospital to confirm the surgical plan. However, the registrar couldn't get hold of the consultant. However, remember that evening I have documented I had spoken to [Dr B], who is a consultant at Chester neonatal unit. I have updated her with all the existing issues and mentioned how stable [Baby I] had been since being transferred to us.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "I clarified with her about the surgical plan as she had discussed with the Alder Hey surgical team and she stated [Baby I] would need a contrast study. This procedure involves a dye being inserted via the tummy to see how the dye goes into the gut and X-rays would then be taken and this would allow them to confirm if there is any narrowing in the bowel at any point or any obstruction. [Dr B] advised she would be sorting out the contrast studies either at Alder Hey or Liverpool Women's Hospital. She was happy to have the baby back the following day on the basis of the information given. The transport team were informed of the required transport for the following day. There were no issues overnight and gases remained good. Oxygen requirement was down and she remained stable.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "As this was not the first episode and she had been conservatively managed previously, this is why we suspected there may be issues with the stricture, which is not unusual after necrotising enterocolitis. However, no stricture was found and her treatment received is routine treatment for necrotising enterocolitis.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "The following morning, on 17 October 2015, at 9 am, my colleague, Dr Lee, was working and again she spoke to a consultant at the Countess of Chester Hospital. This was Chester consultant [Dr C] and it was confirmed again the circumstances around the transfer of [Baby I] back to Chester and [Dr C] has also agreed to the return to Chester for [Baby I]. She left here at around 11.00 hours on 17 October back to Chester."
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.speaker: HUDSON

blocks.text: So that's a gauge, is it, of the functionality of the line and its interaction with the baby?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HUDSON

blocks.text: A zero score is the optimum score?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Perfect, yes.
blocks.speaker: HUDSON

blocks.text: So the pressure was between 270 and 300 at times. Does it follow from the remainder of your sentence here that that was sub-optimal, so you addressed it by repositioning the line?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes, that's correct.
blocks.speaker: HUDSON

blocks.text: "TPN and lipid running as prescribed."
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Through the long line?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HUDSON

blocks.text: "Rates increased at midnight due to weight gain."
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Can you expand on that for us?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Fluids are worked out in millilitres per kilogram.
blocks.speaker: HUDSON

blocks.text: Quite often the standard is 150ml per kilogram of weight for the baby. As the baby grows, we increase that to reflect the weight gain.
blocks.speaker: HUDSON

blocks.text: Thank you. So it was upped, increased, as your note tells us:
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: "New TPN and lipid in situ."
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: So the nutrition, as it were, was attached to the long line?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HUDSON

blocks.text: "Free drainage via NGT, minimal aspirates recorded. Clear fluid."
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Could you expand upon that sentence, please?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes. Free drainage just refers to -- there's a couple of ways that we do it. Sometimes we leave a feeding syringe without the plunger in attached to the end of the tube and hang it up so that any kind of aspirates or air can come out of the stomach without disturbing the baby. Other times there will be a bag attached so if any fluids were to come out of the stomach they'd go into the bag. But it appears in this situation minimal aspirates are recorded, not much was coming out.
blocks.speaker: HUDSON

blocks.text: Thank you. You examined the baby's abdomen, it would seem?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HUDSON

blocks.text: And we know from your evidence last week that [Baby I] was a baby who had presented at times with a distended abdomen —
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HUDSON

blocks.text: -- and that was something that you knew about?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HUDSON

blocks.text: And you were alert to, it would seem?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HUDSON

blocks.text: On this occasion you recorded it was both soft and nondistended.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HUDSON

blocks.text: She was, it would seem, unsettled at the start of the shift and rooting.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HUDSON

blocks.text: We know at this point in time she was nil by mouth; is that right?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: That's correct.
blocks.speaker: HUDSON

blocks.text: And you settled her with a dummy?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HUDSON

blocks.text: And she was sleeping at the time you made that note at 03.11 and when awake she was alert?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HUDSON

blocks.text: So putting all those component parts together, on your assessment, upon your being reunited with [Baby I] after a break, how was she?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: From what I recall, she looked very well, she looked, I would say, better than I'd seen her for a while previously. Like I've noted, I've said she's pink and well perfused -- I didn't say pale pink, I've said pink.
blocks.speaker: HUDSON

blocks.text: Her colour was much better. Her abdomen was soft, it was nondistended, which, as we've already talked about, often it was distended and quite full, sometimes quite veiny looking. So in all she was a very stable baby considering what had happened in the weeks prior.
blocks.speaker: HUDSON

blocks.text: You explain that notwithstanding the location, both within an incubator and within nursery 1, that she wasn't classed as an intensive care baby. What classification of neonate patient was she?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: I imagine she would still be classed as HDU. I think when she first came back to us, I think she was on a high flow device, alongside the central line, which would definitely make her a high dependency. I don't recall 100%, but it might well be that because there's kind of IV nutrition and a central line in situ she would still be classed as high dependency because you are having to check that line every hour. It's an increased workload.
blocks.speaker: HUDSON

blocks.text: Thank you. But for the cautious approach being taken because of her rocky history, would she -- as a high dependency baby, where would she otherwise have been located?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Nursery 2.
blocks.speaker: HUDSON

blocks.text: Did anything of note happen during your night shift of the 21st into the 22nd?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Not that I recall.
blocks.speaker: HUDSON

blocks.text: You were next on duty the following day?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HUDSON

blocks.text: Were you aware that there were communications between the Countess of Chester and Alder Hey in relation to the possibility of a barium enema procedure being undertaken with [Baby I]?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes, I was.
blocks.speaker: HUDSON

blocks.text: Was that being dealt with on an urgent basis or was it being dealt with on a conditional basis dependent upon her progress?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: From what I recall, from our perspective, on the neonatal unit it was urgent because of her history and what had happened and us not having a particular answer for why she'd been so sick. But we are very much, when dealing with a
blocks.speaker: HUDSON

blocks.text: hospital, at the mercy of their beds and what other patients they've got coming through the door.
blocks.speaker: HUDSON

blocks.text: So from our point of view it was urgent but it wasn't an emergency case.
blocks.speaker: HUDSON

blocks.text: Thank you. Could we move forward then to 22 October.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Could we go, please, Mr Murphy, to tile 48, which merely records the fact that there was a handover at the usual time and that you began to make -- take over the care, details of which you noted retrospectively.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HUDSON

blocks.text: Could we click on that tile for a moment, please?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Page 14954. Look at the bottom left of that page, please:
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: "Written for care taken over at 19.45 hours."
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Do we read that literally, that you literally took over care at 19.45?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HUDSON

blocks.text: Can you infer anything from the fact that it was 19.45 as opposed to 20.00 hours, as we sometimes see with a night shift starting?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: I think because I'd taken care of her the day prior, the night prior, I don't think there was a great deal to hand over in that time. She remained quite stable, well in herself, so handover would have been fairly concise.
blocks.speaker: HUDSON

blocks.text: That's probably why.
blocks.speaker: HUDSON

blocks.text: So just to explain that a little further, when you say not a great deal to hand over, do you mean not a great deal of information?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HUDSON

blocks.text: So as is the protocol, we know, you began by checking all equipment and satisfying yourself that it was all satisfactory; is that right?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HUDSON

blocks.text: Then you considered her charts or did you start to make entry in the charts?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: I can see that I detailed some observations at 8 pm.
blocks.speaker: HUDSON

blocks.text: Thank you. So if we look back -- return rather to the paper document, the -- where do we find your 8 pm observations? Is that overleaf at page J15035?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes, that's the one.
blocks.speaker: HUDSON

blocks.text: So we can see your initials appear once and once only on that chart?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HUDSON

blocks.text: And they correspond to 20.00 hours, 8 pm, at which point her heart rate was?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Heart rate was around 135.
blocks.speaker: HUDSON

blocks.text: Is that satisfactory?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes, very much so.
blocks.speaker: HUDSON

blocks.text: Respirations?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Respirations around 50, again satisfactory.
blocks.speaker: HUDSON

blocks.text: Temperature?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Temperature is about 36.8/36.9, which again is optimal.
blocks.speaker: HUDSON

blocks.text: Sats?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Saturations 96% in air, which again is optimal.
blocks.speaker: HUDSON

blocks.text: Next, O2, your predecessor, Caroline Oakley, has put some digits but you have just put the word "air" above your initials?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HUDSON

blocks.text: Does it follow that she, [Baby I], was not receiving any respiratory or ventilatory support of any kind at this point in time?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HUDSON

blocks.text: We can see that somebody, are you able to say whether it was you or not, has entered 23.00 hours for the time?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes, that was me.
blocks.speaker: HUDSON

blocks.text: But not entered any observations taken beneath that --
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: HUDSON

blocks.text: -- time column? Are you able to help us as to why not?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes. It was -- the long line had stopped working, had to be flushed and then later removed, and then [Baby I] had had to be re-cannulated by the doctor. So I think that had happened in that time period, between kind of like quarter past 10 and 11. So if you have got a patient who's just had a procedure done you wouldn't necessarily record observations at that time because they might be unsettled or they might not be accurate so you'd leave them for a little bit to rest, basically.
blocks.speaker: HUDSON

blocks.text: Is that because the procedure may have unsettled them and disturbed the observations?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes, potentially.
blocks.speaker: HUDSON

blocks.text: So let's look at your note:
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: "Observations satisfactory as charted."
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Then:
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: "[Baby I] was unsettled and rooting at the start of shift."
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: But you managed to settle her with a dummy and the containment holding technique?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HUDSON

blocks.text: Then we get to the event that you've just explained to us. Her long line was removed due to constant occlusions, which is lack of flow?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HUDSON

blocks.text: You were assisted by your colleague Lucy Letby; is that right?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HUDSON

blocks.text: Who was unable to flush through the long line?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HUDSON

blocks.text: And therefore did you seek assistance from the registrar, Dr Chang?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes, that's correct.
blocks.speaker: HUDSON

blocks.text: What happened as per your record there?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: I think Dr Chang had come and pulled the dressing back, tried to reposition the line, so in these circumstances you can't insert the line any further because it's been outside the body, but you can pull it back. So from my notes I can see she'd attempted that, tried to flush it, it didn't work, so we did remove a line in the end.
blocks.speaker: HUDSON

blocks.text: Thank you. And was at least, for an intended temporary measure, a cannula sited in [Baby I]'s right foot?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HUDSON

blocks.text: Before we consider that, I've skipped over -- upon removal of the long line, was the site of the long line examined?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HUDSON

blocks.text: And did you detect anything that may have suggested that [Baby I] had been troubled by that long line?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: HUDSON

blocks.text: So no oedema, no swelling, yes --
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Exactly, yes.
blocks.speaker: HUDSON

blocks.text: -- and no duskiness? What would duskiness be indicative of?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: You're looking at discolouration of a limb, less common in long lines than umbilical lines. It's just essentially important to make sure that you are happy that the perfusion of the limb hasn't been affected by the line itself and that's why I've documented that it's completely normal.
blocks.speaker: HUDSON

blocks.text: Thank you. So was the provision of nutrition transferred from the long line, which now had been removed, to the cannula?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: The clear liquid, the TPN, was. The lipid, which supplies the fats, was stopped because that's not able to be given peripherally.
blocks.speaker: HUDSON

blocks.text: Right. As you said:
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: "Lipids stopped until long line could be sited."
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: New sentence.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: "High pressures via this initially, then reduced on repositioning."
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: What's the "this" in that sentence?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: High pressures via the cannula.
blocks.speaker: HUDSON

blocks.text: Thank you. Was that just to get things moving?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HUDSON

blocks.text: And did they move satisfactorily?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes, they did.
blocks.speaker: HUDSON

blocks.text: The remainder of this note tells us how [Baby I] reacted, if at all, to this procedure.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HUDSON

blocks.text: She tolerated it very well?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HUDSON

blocks.text: "Sucrose offered but..."
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: And then if we go to the top of the other side of the single page, so top right:
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: "Sucrose offered but [Baby I] happy with dummy. [Baby I] pink and well perfused at this time, awake and alert."
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Can you just talk us through "sucrose offered but [Baby I] happy with dummy"?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Sucrose is what we use often if it's a painful procedure, uncomfortable procedure for babies. It's essentially sugary water. I think the thought process is it acts on receptors to offer pain relief. You'd offer it, she already had a dummy in her mouth. If she's happy with the dummy, you'd kind of offer, but if they don't -- you'd expect them to suck on the applicator as if they were having a dummy or if they were having a bottle. I think in this case she was happy just to stay with a dummy so I didn't push it any further.
blocks.speaker: HUDSON

blocks.text: Taking a step back from the notes for a moment, I'm going to ask you to tell us a little about [Baby I] as a patient in this sort of context. Compared to other babies, was [Baby I]
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: a baby, a patient, who was difficult to settle, easy to settle or don't you have an opinion?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: From what I remember of my experience of [Baby I], generally she was quite easy to settle. I think dummy, sucrose, containment holding or being held by family, she generally settled quite quickly. From what I remember in terms of a staff perspective she was quite happy once you put her back into the incubator or cot and just kind of leave her be, she would settle quite nicely.
blocks.speaker: HUDSON

blocks.text: Thank you. So we've got here you explaining why it is that you undertook observations at 20.00 hours, had endorsed the chart in anticipation of making more observations at 23.00 hours, but because of this, that you have just described to us, you elected not to --
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HUDSON

blocks.text: -- at 23.00 hours, at 11 pm?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Now we're going to shortly go to your notes of the events just before midnight. Before we look at the note, if we could turn the screen off for a moment, please. I'm going to ask you what you actually remember about this as opposed to what you have recorded retrospectively.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Okay.
blocks.speaker: HUDSON

blocks.text: Do you recall the events approaching midnight on this night shift?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes, I do.
blocks.speaker: HUDSON

blocks.text: What's the first feature of this event that you recollect?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: I remember -- I think it was just prior to midnight, I think [Baby I] was unsettled, crying, so I had attended to her in the incubator to try and settle her. I think I tried the usual measures of containment holding, the dummy, sucrose. It didn't seem to work. She was very unsettled, it was quite a relentless cry. So the last thing I tried was to reposition her on to her tummy, which sometimes would settle her. On this occasion it didn't.
blocks.speaker: HUDSON

blocks.text: Pause there if you would, please, Ms Hudson. She was unsettled and so you tried to address it first by offering her sucrose?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Mm-hm.
blocks.speaker: HUDSON

blocks.text: It might be obvious to you, but if you can explain to us your thought process there.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: I think in [Baby I]'s case, because she wasn't receiving any milk feeds, what we would do sometimes to settle her was give sucrose. Although she's not having a procedure, she is uncomfortable, and generally speaking you would usually feed a baby in this instance, but we couldn't. Sucrose is absorbed buccally, in the gum, so there usually isn't any danger of giving it to a baby who's not having any other oral feeds, so it's a comfort measure.
blocks.speaker: HUDSON

blocks.text: Right. It didn't work?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: HUDSON

blocks.text: So next effort on your part?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: I don't remember the sequence, but I'd offered the dummy, containment holding, and generally it used to work. After those didn't work, I repositioned her.
blocks.speaker: HUDSON

blocks.text: She'd been lying on her back, face up. And I repositioned her on her tummy with her head to the side, to see if that settled her.
blocks.speaker: HUDSON

blocks.text: When you say generally it used to work, do you mean generally with all babies or generally with [Baby I] or both?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Generally with [Baby I], generally with most babies, but every baby is an individual. It did tend to work with [Baby I].
blocks.speaker: HUDSON

blocks.text: But not on this occasion?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: HUDSON

blocks.text: She continued to express in a way that you deemed that she was very unsettled?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HUDSON

blocks.text: We will look at your notes for that phrase, which we'll go to in due course. Was she crying?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HUDSON

blocks.text: Were you familiar with [Baby I]'s cry?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HUDSON

blocks.text: Was this bout of crying typical of [Baby I] or atypical?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: In my experience, atypical.
blocks.speaker: HUDSON

blocks.text: Could you expand upon that, please?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Um... It was... It was a type of cry that I hadn't myself experienced her make before. It was very loud -- it was, like I said, relentless, almost constant. There was no stopping and starting. There was no fluctuation.
blocks.speaker: HUDSON

blocks.text: It was just constantly very loud and something that I'd not heard from her before.
blocks.speaker: HUDSON

blocks.text: You can't, you told us in fairness, be sure of the sequence, but you tried the sucrose, the dummy, you tried containment holding and you tried repositioning?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HUDSON

blocks.text: Was repositioning the last --
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes, it was.
blocks.speaker: HUDSON

blocks.text: -- attempt?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HUDSON

blocks.text: And what happened upon repositioning [Baby I]?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: She then, within seconds of putting her on her tummy, became very quiet and I noticed that she was having pauses in her breathing. I can't remember exactly what I'd -- the sequence, but I had turned her back over and shouted for help around the same time and that's when Lucy came in to give me assistance.
blocks.speaker: HUDSON

blocks.text: So on repositioning, she stopped crying, but not in a way that satisfied you that you'd achieved your objective?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: HUDSON

blocks.text: Was there a problem at this stage?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HUDSON

blocks.text: Was she being monitored at this stage?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HUDSON

blocks.text: And what did those monitors tell you?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: I can't remember without kind of looking at what I've written.
blocks.speaker: HUDSON

blocks.text: In general terms?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: In general terms, I think her observations started to dip, so her oxygen levels started to decrease and her heart rate had started to drift as well. That's when, just prior to seeing that on the monitor, I'd called for help after she'd gone quiet, and then we got her in position for giving ventilation breaths.
blocks.speaker: HUDSON

blocks.text: "We" being?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Myself and Lucy.
blocks.speaker: HUDSON

blocks.text: And having positioned her for ventilation and breaths, did you say --
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HUDSON

blocks.text: -- was she provided with assistance --
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HUDSON

blocks.text: -- in that regard? What did the two of you do and who did what?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: I don't recall who did what now, but we start with airway always. So we'd have positioned her airway in a neutral position, given oxygen to begin with, and then would have progressed to ventilation breaths had she not made any effort herself. And then I think after an initial period of -- I don't know how long -- less than a minute of her not really responding and recognising that it was an acute episode, we called for further help and crash bleeped the paediatric doctors who were on that evening.
blocks.speaker: HUDSON

blocks.text: We will have their notes and we'll hear from Dr Chang in due course. But let's go back to your nursing note of this phase of the evening:
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: "[Baby I] very unsettled."
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: You queried whether it was due to hunger. You recorded the efforts you made to no effect.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HUDSON

blocks.text: She was placed prone because, in your experience, from previous nursing of [Baby I], that would usually settle her:
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: "She became very quiet, apnoeic, dusky in appearance."
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Do you remember that?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HUDSON

blocks.text: Is that indicative of poor perfusion?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HUDSON

blocks.text: With the help of Lucy Letby, you repositioned [Baby I] on to her back, Neopuffed, and there are your data.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Applied due to colour and stop... cessation of breathing, but to no avail because the colour didn't improve --
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HUDSON

blocks.text: -- and her sats and heart rate began -- perhaps continued -- to drop rapidly. You increased the amount of assistance being given with no effect, so no doubt in consequence there was a crash bleep sounded and the paediatricians attended?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HUDSON

blocks.text: Cardiac compressions began at around midnight. Was that by the doctors or you or both?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: I can't recall.
blocks.speaker: HUDSON

blocks.text: You can't recall. Dr Gibbs was called and he attended, and we'll hear from Dr Gibbs in due course.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HUDSON

blocks.text: And at this point your records suggest that [Baby I] was intubated, placed on a ventilator, whilst awaiting chest X-ray?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HUDSON

blocks.text: "Prior to ventilation, [Baby I] had become more alert and crying."
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: So was that post-intubation?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: That was, I think, post-intubation but prior to being connected to the ventilator, was still receiving manual assistance.
blocks.speaker: HUDSON

blocks.text: Then your note reflects, back prior to the resuscitation, when you noted, new sentence:
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: "Her abdomen was soft and non-distended prior to resus, no change from handover."
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HUDSON

blocks.text: So was that meant to inform we the readers of her condition from 8 pm until this event, this acute event, approaching midnight?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes, it was.
blocks.speaker: HUDSON

blocks.text: And you refer us to the clinical notes, which the jury will hear about in due course.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: There was an X-ray. Was that the chest X-ray that you referred to in your earlier note?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HUDSON

blocks.text: NAD, no abnormalities detected?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HUDSON

blocks.text: And the medics decided to extubate [Baby I], she having been intubated a little time earlier, as per your note.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: She was, you recorded, quite distressed and working against the ventilator.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HUDSON

blocks.text: So what was that indicative of?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: That she'd recovered quite quickly and ideally what you like with a baby on a ventilator is that they're synchronised with the breaths being given by the machinery. If a baby's working against it, you're not going to get very good oxygenation if you leave them that way and potentially you're going to cause lung damage, which is -- at that point we were making a decision, do we keep her on the ventilator potentially, having to sedate and paralyse her, or do we go by clinical look and take her off, which we did.
blocks.speaker: HUDSON

blocks.text: Thank you. Looking at the remainder of that sentence, on extubation, how was she?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: She was back to how she'd been prior to the event itself. Like I said, she's awake, alert, breathing
blocks.speaker: HUDSON

blocks.text: independently, and cueing for a feed, so seemingly displayed normal behaviour despite what had just happened.
blocks.speaker: HUDSON

blocks.text: The next entry, Mr Murphy. We won't go there now.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: So there was this acute event and we'll read that you, as her designated nurse, reported this event to her parents.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: I don't remember how long, it was all very quick. Maybe within 30 minutes, I think, between -- it was a very quick resuscitation, it wasn't prolonged, there was no drugs given, and I don't think she was connected to the ventilator for very long. I'm not sure, you'd have to look at the timestamps of Xrays and things.
blocks.speaker: HUDSON

blocks.text: It's unfair of me to ask that when the clinical notes will tell us no doubt in due course.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Afterwards.

blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HUDSON

blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.

blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.speaker: HUDSON

blocks.speaker: DRIVER

But I was nearby to hear the monitor, which I think is why I went into the room for this event.

blocks.speaker: DRIVER

At which point Lucy was already with her, trying to comfort her, trying to settle her, and at that point in time her observations were normal, she wasn't desaturating, she wasn't bradycardic, and like I say she was crying, so she wasn't apnoeic.
blocks.speaker: HUDSON

blocks.text: Pausing there, and considering the two possibilities that you just alluded to, you were alerted, you say, either by an alarm sounding on the monitor, yes --
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.

blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HUDSON

blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.speaker: HUDSON

blocks.text: So taking those various pieces of equipment as one, what changes in the baby could potentially trigger an alarm?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: So there are parameters that are set in these monitors, they might be slightly different per baby. If an observation -so saturations, respiratory rate, heart rate -- falls outside of those set parameters the monitor will alarm. Depending on the severity and how far outside those parameters it is, it will alarm with an orange alarm and an orange colour will flash or a red colour will flash. Both of them are equally as loud, but one is slightly faster than the other.
blocks.speaker: HUDSON

blocks.text: So a fall in any of those vital signs, if I might use that phrase --
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Or a rise.
blocks.speaker: HUDSON

blocks.text: -- or a rise, quite so -- could potentially have triggered one or more of the alarms?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HUDSON

blocks.text: But you can't be sure, is this fair, whether it was the alarm or [Baby I] --
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HUDSON

blocks.text: -- that caught your attention? You re-entered nursery 1 and Nurse Letby was there at [Baby I]'s -- well, where was she?

blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HUDSON

blocks.text: What sort of cry?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.speaker: HUDSON

blocks.text: What did you think?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: My initial concern was, despite the fact that at that point in time her heart rate wasn't bradycardic, she was obviously breathing, her saturations were satisfactory, my concern was that because this sound, this cry, was the same that she was going to have another episode. My only reason being for that is that I had not heard it before and when she'd done it previously she'd then had a collapse. That was my concern.
blocks.speaker: HUDSON

blocks.text: Did you articulate that concern?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HUDSON

blocks.text: To whom?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Lucy.
blocks.speaker: HUDSON

blocks.text: How soon after re-entering nursery 1 did you make mention of that concern?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Within, I would say, about 60 seconds of being there, after kind of hearing the sound for slightly longer and kind of
blocks.speaker: HUDSON

blocks.text: looking at her and seeing that she wasn't interested in the dummy that was being offered. That's when I said, something along the lines of, "She's going to do it again, it's the same cry", something like that.
blocks.speaker: HUDSON

blocks.text: So whatever actual words you used was an expression, was it, of concern that the events of an hour or so earlier were about to repeat?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HUDSON

blocks.text: And you said that to Lucy Letby?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HUDSON

blocks.text: Did she respond?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HUDSON

blocks.text: What did she say?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: I think Lucy was trying to reassure me and just said, "She just needs to settle, she just needs to settle".
blocks.speaker: HUDSON

blocks.text: I think from previous experience, she would have, but it's just because I had heard that sound previously.
blocks.speaker: HUDSON

blocks.text: When you heard it previously an hour earlier, were you alone or were you with anybody else?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: I was alone to begin with until I shouted for help, at which point that's when Lucy had entered the room after she'd already stopped breathing.
blocks.speaker: HUDSON

blocks.text: What happened next?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Um... The events happened similar to the event prior: she had this relentless cry, we couldn't settle her, and then she became quiet, began to have slow pauses in breathing, and her heart rate started to drift down, become bradycardic, and her saturations started to drift.
blocks.speaker: HUDSON

blocks.text: How did you respond to this deterioration?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: We initiated oxygen delivery again. We hadn't started compressions at this point because I think they were 70 to 80, her heart rate, and we'd given some stimulation and I think started airway management, so ventilation breaths, and from what I recall beyond that, shouted for further help from one of our colleagues and then at that point I knew that the medical team were in the room next door waiting for a delivery, so rather
blocks.speaker: HUDSON

blocks.text: than put out a crash bleep, I ran through the double doors to alert them to the situation once Chris had entered the room.
blocks.speaker: HUDSON

blocks.text: Is that Nurse Christopher Booth?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HUDSON

blocks.text: Is he the colleague you referred to a moment or two ago?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.

blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.

blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HUDSON

blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HUDSON

blocks.text: And did you bring her to [Baby I]'s aid?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HUDSON

blocks.text: As per the last event, Dr Chang took over immediate management of the problem?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HUDSON

blocks.text: But shortly thereafter, was Dr Gibbs called --
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HUDSON

blocks.text: -- to give yet more assistance?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.

blocks.text: If we go to tile 144, please. We see that that was within minutes. We're now at 01.18.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: At tiles 146 and 147, we'll see that Dr Gibbs was there again shortly thereafter at 01.22 hours, according to the swipe data.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Did Dr Gibbs lead a very prolonged resuscitation attempt?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes, he did.

blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes, I did.

blocks.text: And Dr Gibbs will tell us all the detail of that, so I needn't go through it with you, Ms Hudson. We all know tragically that it was all to no avail and that [Baby I] passed away.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.

blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: I don't think I did directly. blocks.speaker: HUDSON

blocks.text: Very well. There's one more part of your note that I invite you to assist us with, please, and that's behind tile 207.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: To the bottom of the right of that page, please. In the previous paragraph, you'd described the dramatic events that we've just touched upon, but then in retrospect, you wrote at 06.25 the following:
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: "Asterisk. NGT on free drainage, produced 2ml."
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.

blocks.text: So that was in reference to, I think, the second event.

blocks.text: It's good practice in a resus, if you can, to have a nasogastric tube in situ, so if you're giving ventilation breaths via a Neopuff and not an ET tube, some air will inevitably get in through the oesophagus into the stomach, so you aspirate the NG as much as you can. blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.speaker: HUDSON

blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: I think that was in relation to both. On the previous occasion I'd been asked where staff were sat when I'd asked them to listen out for her, which was at the desk, and then also when I was outside of the nursery where I would have been sat.

blocks.speaker: DRIVER
