Ms Hudson, what you have described to us will have been an upsetting experience for you and for other people involved with it. I just want to make it plain, everyone understands that. Also for those close to [Baby I] and her family too.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: So the questions I'm going to ask, which may sometimes seem a little technical, are not asked with any lack of sympathy for what took place. Okay?
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HUDSON

blocks.text: When you last came to give evidence, you were telling us about events on the night of 13 October; do you recall that?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HUDSON

blocks.text: When you came to look after [Baby I] on the nights that we're dealing with today, you knew at that point that in between then there'd been further collapses and arrests, didn't you?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HUDSON

blocks.text: And you knew that some time around the 15th to 17 October, [Baby I] had been transferred to Arrowe Park and then brought back to the Countess of Chester; is that right?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: That's correct.
blocks.speaker: HUDSON

blocks.text: And certainly your understanding was that she'd been very ill at the time she had gone to the Arrowe Park Hospital, hadn't she?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HUDSON

blocks.text: You have described how [Baby I] presented so far as you could see on the night that we're dealing with --
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HUDSON

blocks.text: -- or the nights that we're dealing with now?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HUDSON

blocks.text: But would you agree a baby like [Baby I] is a baby that does have to be watched closely, however stable she appears?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HUDSON

blocks.text: There is always the potential for a deterioration, isn't there?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HUDSON

blocks.text: An expression that used in your statement, if it comes to mind, is that she's never completely out of the woods, I think is the way that you put it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HUDSON

blocks.text: One of the issues is you can't be complacent because they can be unpredictable in what happens?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes, that was my view at the time.
blocks.speaker: HUDSON

blocks.text: All right. You were asked about the classification of [Baby I] in terms of the care she was receiving.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HUDSON

blocks.text: When I'm putting it that way, that's what I mean about not wanting to sound insensitive, but we understand there are categories of care?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HUDSON

blocks.text: And [Baby I] was high dependency care on this night; is that right?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: That's correct.
blocks.speaker: HUDSON

blocks.text: You explained last time that you were within about the first 8 or 9 months of qualification at this time?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HUDSON

blocks.text: You're a good deal more experienced now, of course.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HUDSON

blocks.text: You, of course, look after the baby that you are allocated to look after, don't you?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HUDSON

blocks.text: So I'm not suggesting you've made any choice as to who you look after or what you're doing, you will do your best to look after whatever baby is yours, won't you?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HUDSON

blocks.text: Just so we can follow, at the time we're dealing with, you wouldn't have been intensive care trained then, would you?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: HUDSON

blocks.text: And is there a special training for being able to do neonatal resuscitation that nurses can take?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: For newborn resuscitations, so that done at delivery, yes.
blocks.speaker: HUDSON

blocks.text: That's a different thing then from this?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HUDSON

blocks.text: Right. Is there particular training for a nurse so that she or he is qualified to handle long lines and that type of procedure?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: There isn't specific training. But generally speaking, at the point that I was then, I was able to care for babies with them, but I wasn't able to use the lines myself.
blocks.speaker: HUDSON

blocks.text: You could care for them --
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HUDSON

blocks.text: -- but you couldn't use them?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Couldn't access them, couldn't flush them, couldn't give drugs by them.
blocks.speaker: HUDSON

blocks.text: Is that one of the reasons why when the line had to be dealt with later on the evening of the 22nd, Nurse Letby and then Dr Chang had to be involved with that?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HUDSON

blocks.text: Again, just looking at the period we're dealing with, these couple of nights, the 21st and 22 October, was [Baby I] nil by mouth at that time?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HUDSON

blocks.text: So she was receiving nutrition by the long line; is that correct?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HUDSON

blocks.text: Well, I think we can all understand the word "rooting" is used a lot, not just by you but by another nurse.

blocks.text: Can you explain -- those of us who have contact with babies, from what we can remember of it, you know how babies sometimes are demanding, they appear to want feeding.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HUDSON

blocks.text: Can you just describe what this rooting gesture in [Baby I]'s case was that you're talking about?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Yes. So rooting is a classical sign of when a baby is asking for food. It usually happens before they start to cry. It's an early stage of hunger communication, and usually it's characterised by the baby's head moving from side to side, sometimes a little rapidly, and they tend to stick their tongue out and smack their lips a lot. It's a very specific behaviour that occurs when they're hungry.
